If you are a technologist/generalist, aiming for small companies is a good strategy. If you're not in SV even better, you may end up in a real grass roots business and a really interesting problem domain that is ostensibly Not Software.

I personally, cannot stand the software for software industry. You, me, we have all built such arbitrary bullshit machines that link together in a web of unnecessary business. We lambast redundant jobs and useless management, but a moment of reflection for our industry and just how much software we have built for entirely self-serving purposes. So many man hours spent on the ephemeral whims of software. Sorry for the cynicism.

Less cynically, I feel the smaller the company, self-funded, the more likely a generalist will thrive and the business domain will be real-world and impactful. If it's venture funded and can pivot to advertising, it probably will. If you move away from tech hubs the wages are lower, but you might find a more fulfilling role.

This post seems to take the stance that we need to cultivate failure so that we can learn. We don’t need to cultivate failure, there’s plenty of failure to be had. I mean people need to be allowed to make their own mistakes but that’s not the same thing.

“How do we solve this?”

By hiring other people who actually know what they’re doing - product managers, marketers, designers, etc - and then, here’s the crucial part: listening to them. There are a whole set of people who are _not_ technologists, who do things that are _not_ building shiny widgets, and who have skills that are useful nonetheless and that we cannot trivially replicate just by thinking about it a lot.

As a side note, I find it interesting the way people will write explicitly about their job experience at companies like this, naming where they work, dropping anecdotes about the CEO, about colleagues.

To borrow John Cale's rephrasing of a proverb:

"Meet me on the staircase on the way down; we'll see if there's been a mistake".

I talk about where I have worked; I have in the past written about it. But I find it interesting how people don't seem to grasp that often you should change the names to protect the incompetent or guilty, and should probably avoid simply spilling out anecdotes that an LLM will thread together.

Don't get yourself a reputation for being indiscreet simply for a blog post.

> We were downstream of the business model; our job was simply to wait and prepare for its eventual success.

Hard thing to learn and to stomach. The you are essentially a few nodes downstream from the decision makers who commissioned the software in the first place. They have some long-term view even if you can identify in the short-term that things won't be working out well long-term. Hard to reconcile that with a steady paycheck.

You can then get yourself into product decisions, to try to steer the direction a bit, working wirh sales, but that has all its own issues too (the article mentions "selling whatever we thought would entice the salespeople enticing the salespeople enticing the brands." at one workplace)

How does anyone find fulfillment when this is the long-term prospect at most companies for software?

Get out from under the VC playbook and start asking yourself and the people around you what should exist. What is the world missing? Use AI as your cofounder as prototype with basic tech - html, css, js, sqlite. Gain traction. See the truth about the audience by doing your own customer service. Then when you find something with true traction, talk about scaling it. You will learn far more and do better.

I think it's because technologists are easier to manage.

Product engineers, on the other hand, are actually quite ambiguous to evaluate. Many methodologies have been introduced, starting from Barry Boehm, but over time they gradually stop fitting, and there are many points that are hard to assess. It's essentially a matter of organizational management theory. The ideal of organizational management theory is that diversity comes together to create synergy, but conversely, such diversity means that decision-making within the organization slows down.

Technologists, by contrast, are very easy to observe in terms of speed or code quality. In fact, most people choose a career of learning technology and making money rather than founding a startup, and from that perspective, since "career" tends to be emphasized as an employee's career rather than a founder's career, isn't that why technologists are emphasized?

What companies value as a capability is ultimately an evaluation that can be measured. And product engineering, when you think about it, presupposes discussions with decision makers.

'Is it necessary to implement this feature?'

'Do customers actually need this feature?'

'Isn't the business model wrong?'

Most decision makers are people high up in the hierarchy, and friction with them is unavoidable. In other words, it crosses existing role boundaries, which means more frequent conflicts in organizational dynamics.

Whether that is ultimately a gain or a loss for the organization is something nobody can konw
